Consider a plane electromagnetic wave traveling in free space along the $z$-direction, where the electric and magnetic fields are given by $\mathbf{E} = E_0 e^{i(kz - \omega t)}\hat{i}$ and $\mathbf{H} = H_0 e^{i(kz - \omega t)}\hat{j}$.

From Maxwell's curl equation in free space ($\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$), we evaluate:
$$\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ E_x & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \frac{\partial E_x}{\partial z} \hat{j} = i k E_0 e^{i(kz - \omega t)}\hat{j}$$

Equating this to $-\mu_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial t} = i\omega \mu_0 H_0 e^{i(kz - \omega t)}\hat{j}$, we obtain $kE_0 = \omega \mu_0 H_0$. 

Taking the divergence of $\mathbf{E}$ in free space ($\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0$):
$$\frac{\partial E_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial E_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial E_z}{\partial z} = 0 \implies 0 + 0 + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(E_0 e^{i(kz - \omega t)}) = 0$$
Since $ikE_0 \neq 0$, the propagation direction must satisfy $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0$ and $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{H} = 0$. This proves that both $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ are perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation ($\mathbf{k}$), establishing the transverse nature of electromagnetic waves.
proTip: Always state Maxwell's equations first as the starting point for proving wave properties.
